title: Memory-assisted advantage for state transfer in disordered quantum many-body scar system
abstract: We analyze how memory in disorder facilitates quantum communication in many-body scar systems. We consider three distinct types of disorder, viz., memoryful, and memoryless uniform and Gaussian, and compare their respective performances in facilitating quantum state transfer. Using the maximum transfer fidelity and fidelity area as figures of merit, we find that memoryful disorder yields a better performance than the memoryless disordered channels. Furthermore, the maximum transfer fidelity exhibits an initial parabolic decay with disorder strength, followed by a linear decrease, for all the disorder models considered. We introduce a degree of scarness, and show that it is higher for memoryful disorder in comparison to memoryless disorders, implying a role of scarness in the quantum state transfer protocol. We further perform a scaling analysis, revealing that memory effect in disorder is not only beneficial for short-distance but also long-distance quantum state transfer. Finally, we show that the state yielding the maximum transfer fidelity has larger inverse participation ratio for memoryful disorder in comparison to the other two disorders, highlighting the role of nonergodicity in enhancing state transfer.
summary: The paper analyzes Quantum State Transfer in disordered many-body scar systems, comparing memoryful disorder against memoryless types. It finds that the presence of 'memory' in the disorder significantly boosts state transfer fidelity and robustness. This enhancement is linked to increased scarness and nonergodicity, suggesting a mechanism for designing quantum channels resistant to noise.
main_problem: The study investigates how incorporating 'memory' into disorder affects quantum communication, specifically Quantum State Transfer (QST), within many-body scar systems.
main_result: Memoryful disorder significantly enhances QST performance compared to memoryless disorders (uniform or Gaussian). This enhancement is correlated with a higher degree of scarness and larger Inverse Participation Ratios (IPR) for the optimal state.
method: The analysis compares different disorder types using fidelity measures ($ ar{F}_M$, $ ar{F}_A$) and performs finite-size scaling analyses on these metrics. It also calculates the IPR to diagnose nonergodicity effects.
model_or_system: The system is a one-dimensional many-body scar system governed by a complex Hamiltonian involving nearest-neighbor couplings and three-body interaction terms, subjected to disorder modeled as memoryful or memoryless (uniform/Gaussian).
key_observables: Maximum transfer fidelity ($ ar{F}_M$), Fidelity Area ($ ar{F}_A$), Degree of Scarness ($ ar{S}$), Inverse Participation Ratio ($	ext{IPRM}$, $	ext{IPRA}$).
important_parameters: Disorder strength ($\sigma$), System size ($L$), and the type of disorder (memoryful vs. memoryless).
main_assumptions: The analysis assumes that higher scarness and nonergodicity, promoted by memoryful disorder, are key factors enhancing state transfer fidelity.
figures_summary: Figures illustrate QST schematics, show the decay of $ ar{F}_M$ and $ ar{F}_A$ vs. disorder strength ($\sigma$), plot $ ar{S}$ vs. $\sigma$, and display scaling analysis results for $ ar{F}_M$ and $ ar{F}_A$ with system size $L$.
paper_structure: The paper systematically compares three disorder types, quantifying performance using fidelity metrics, analyzing the role of scarness via revival measurements, and finally confirming the benefit of memory effects through scaling analysis and IPR calculations.
why_interesting: This work directly addresses how structured randomness (memory) can stabilize quantum information transfer in complex many-body systems, which is crucial for understanding robust quantum computation protocols in realistic noisy environments.
